utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Before we begin our business today, there are a number of outstanding matters concerning the admission of certain exhibits tendered by both parties, and the Chamber will issue its decisions on those now. I will first deal with the approach of the Chamber to the admission of evidence through a witness, which arose particularly during the testimony of Mrs. Zaimovic. On 6th May 2010, the Chamber set out a number of principles for the admission of exhibits tendered through witnesses in line with the practice of other Trial Chambers at this Tribunal. On 7th May 2010, Mr. Robinson requested the Chamber to revisit its rulings on the admission into evidence of various items through Mrs. Zaimovic and made a number of submissions in support of his request and to, more broadly, lower the threshold for admission. The Chamber has considered Mr. Robinson's request and has decided that it will not reconsider its admissibility decisions made on 6 of May 2010. However, in the interests of clarity, the Chamber will issue a written decision shortly in which it will address Mr. Robinson's submissions and provide additional guidelines that will govern the admissibility of evidence through witnesses in this case. I now turn to the issue of the associated exhibits tendered by the Prosecution in relation to Mr. Harland's amalgamated statement. The Chamber deferred its decision on the admissibility of these associated exhibits, leaving its resolution until addressed the question of reconsideration that I've just outlined. On 6 May 2010, Mr. Robinson requested the Chamber to revisit the admission of associated exhibits for Rule 92 ter witnesses. On 7th of May, 2010, he submitted that 30 associated exhibits tendered by the Prosecution in relation to Mr. Harland do not meet the criteria for admission because the witness has no personal knowledge of them and he cannot speak to them. Mr. Robinson provided a table noting the associated exhibits to which he objected and setting out how Mr. Harland addressed them in his amalgamated statement. The Prosecution provided the Chamber with a similar table. The Chamber has considered the parties' submissions. It recalls that the test that it must apply in relation to the admission into evidence of associated exhibits is that, in addition to the basic requirements pursuant to Rule 89(C), each item must "form an inseparable and indispensable part of the testimony." The Chamber will admit into evidence all the associated exhibits tendered in relation to Mr. Harland, with it has not already done in court, with the exception of following that are not admitted into evidence: Rule 65 ter number 30884, an intercept. While the witness has confirmed its contents, the intercept has not been authenticated. The Chamber sees no reason to distinguish the admissibility of this intercept with other intercepts of which the Chamber has previously denied the admission on the basis that the accused can cross-examine the witness about this intercept, as was argued by the Prosecution in its table. Rule 65 ter numbers 19022, 13416 and 13452. Despite stating that he recognised the alleged author's handwriting, Mr. Harland is not in a position to authenticate them, and therefore the Chamber is not satisfied at this time of their reliability. Rule 65 ter number 11780. The Chamber is not satisfied that this document forms an inseparable and indispensable part of Mr. Harland's amalgamated statement as the paragraph where the document is mentioned is not linked at all to any specific aspect of Mr. Harland's evidence contained in the surrounding paragraphs. Rule 65 ter 45204. The Chamber cannot make an assessment of this video as it has not been provided with a copy. However, on the basis of the information provided by the Prosecution about this video, the Chamber will not admit it. In his statement, Mr. Harland mentions the video in paragraph 120, but in its table, the Prosecution refers to a comment by Serb leaders in paragraph 100. While the subject matter of the two may be broadly similar, the video cannot be said to form an inseparable and indispensable part of Mr. Harland's amalgamated statement. Rule 65 ter number 17509. This is a duplicate of Exhibit P781 and so does not need to be admitted for a second time. The Chamber notes that it is open to the Prosecution to put these items to Mr. Harland should it so wish, in any redirect it may have. Should it do so, Mr. Karadzic, you will be able to cross-examine Mr. Harland on those answers about those items. However, please do not -- please do note that your questions are limited solely to what Mr. Harland says about the particular items put to him. The second matters relates to Exhibit D10 -- no. I will deal with it when we conclude Mr. Harland's evidence. Finally, I said I would address the admissibility of MFI Exhibit D154, which was given MFI status yesterday, along with the issue of admissibility of these other documents. The Chamber has considered the admissibility of this document and has concluded that it will not be admitted as Mr. Harland was unable to say anything about it, including to confirm either its form or the content. The same is true with MFI Exhibit D172, which is a news clipping or a media interview. I'm not sure about the exhibit number, but that can be checked later on. Furthermore, as its content was read out to the transcript, there's no need to admit it in the circumstances. That has been the ruling of the Chamber, and there are a couple of more items to be dealt with when Mr. Harland concludes his evidence. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness enters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wonder if the Court might consider providing the parties with an opportunity to at least briefly address the Chamber on some or a couple of the specific issues that potentially arise out of the proposed additional guidelines. We've had some discussions on that. I think there are a number, at least one or two matters, about which the parties agree that may not be dispositive but we'd certainly like the opportunity to raise it with -- provide as much input as possible, perhaps work toward a form of admissibility in the most collaborative fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Harland. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, the sooner we're done, the sooner we'll go home, both you and me. So it would be a good thing if we deal with matters in less of a literary fashion and more factually, if I can put it that way. 1D1078. Could we call up that, please. This is also a document every yours. I have it here in Serbian. However, that is before you, before you came, rather. It is sent by Mr. Andreev to Mr. Thornberry. I believe that there should be an English original, I'm sure. So this is a document that I have in translation, but it must exist in the original. So it's from Viktor Andreev, February 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to page 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to show how my peace efforts were viewed by your superiors and how they assessed them. So in the first paragraph it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The meeting with the military commanders of all three parties that would be chaired by General Morillon was scheduled for next week. I pointed out the importance of establishing a true cease-fire and seeking a solution for Sarajevo in this period. They came up with an idea for which Karadzic says that was proposed to them by the Russian ambassador in Belgrade about placing Sarajevo under UNPROFOR control with a view to establishing peace in town and delaying a solution. That would involve corridors, joint check-points, patrols, control of resources, and so on. There was also a reference to the green line in Cyprus as an example of a solution. Karadzic said that if that were to happen, there would be peace in town within less than two weeks. It was their understanding that this proposal would not be sustainable if it came from their side, although it is as a solution." Do you agree that we accepted the idea of the Russian ambassador, but we did not present it in public at that point in time because the Muslims would have turned it down? Do you agree that it would be more palatable if it were to come from the UN?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really comment. It was before my -- my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, this is a document of Mr. Andreev's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before we further proceed, the e-court says its original is in B/C/S, so could you tell us what document it is? Who sent to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that was sent by Mr. Viktor Andreev, coordinator for civilian affairs of the BH command, UNPROFOR Kiseljak, and its sent to Cedric Thornberry, deputy head of mission and deputy chief of administration. A copy was sent to General Morillon and to the forward command post, and the subject is meeting with Karadzic. At the top it says, "English translation." So I believe that the original is in English. However, what I received from the EDS is the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course the original is in English. Mr. Reid is just checking to see if it's been uploaded in e-court from our side so that we can have the English version shortly available for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was confused with the BH comment in the first page, and I thought it was something -- ABiH document. I was mistaken. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We've gone back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "When I asked Karadzic about the possible deployment of the Canadian Battalion in the area of Sarajevo, he said that that was a terribly sensitive issue. The presence of NATO troops or of the European Community now on their land when intervention is often being mentioned would not be acceptable, although it would be possible to deploy an Asian or African contingent. Canadians are particularly intolerant towards them," towards the Serbs, that is. "After they saw footage of Canadians training for street fighting and also their record in Sector West."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did no longer see the text and we cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Mr. Harland, may I ask you now, you know that we always gave consent for foreign presence, either civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, UNPROFOR troops were not allowed to be stationed on Serb territory until a group of Russians deployed to Grbavica in 1994. And even crossing Serb territory, the Serbs did not allow Canadian or British troops in Srebrenica, for example, because they explicitly said to us that they wanted weaker troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, since you are able to follow the transcript in English, the interpreters couldn't interpret what you read out from the document since they couldn't see the document and you read so fast. So if you could take a look at the transcript, and then if -- find those parts important, you may wish to read that part again. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's uploaded in e-court, 65 ter 21692, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's the original that's been uploaded. I'm a bit concerned that Dr. Karadzic might be reading -- in fact I don't know what he's reading from if it bears the number ET on the top and it appears -- it's drafted in B/C/S. So I think it would be better for us all and -- sorry, better for us all and more accurate to deal with the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we upload the 65 ter 21692. Yes. This seems to be the correct document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is it. However, I don't see the date. Actually, it looks different, but it may be it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So what I read out was the meeting with the military commanders." It's the next page in English: "[In English] Meeting is scheduled for next week." [Interpretation] That's the paragraph I read. That's what I read and it had to do with this proposal: "[In English] If it was done, these suggestions would not be viable coming from them, though as a solution it is viable." [Interpretation] Then two paragraphs down. Can we scroll down, please. Then it's the next page apparently: "[In English] When I asked Karadzic about the possible deployment of CanBat in Sarajevo area, his response was that the issue was extremely sensitive. To have NATO or European troops on their soil now when intervention is often talked about would not be acceptable, though Asian or African contingent might be possible. Canadians, in particular, are not tolerable to them after having seen footage of Canadian training for street fighting as well as their record in Sector West. Karadzic's primary question on deployment of any force to Serb areas were: Where and why they would be deployed? What with what mandate? And could that mandate be changed without their consent?" [Interpretation] I would like to ask to have the document here while we're clarifying the matter. Mr. Harland, if you remember, all agreements require the agreement of all three parties after all, when UNPROFOR was to come to Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war, it required our consent and we gave it. Do you remember that? In order to come to Bosnia. I'm not talking about deployment in Banja Luka where there was no need to have UNPROFOR presence. We did give our consent to have UNPROFOR come to Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our position was that UNPROFOR did not need the consent of the parties. It was deployed under Chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter. Of course it made it a lot easier if there was consent, but our position was we did not need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not exactly the way it is. Chapter 7 was mentioned a lot later. However, while there was still a war going on in Croatia, UNPROFOR came to Bosnia with our consent, and every peace agreement meant that we had to sign it and that we had to give our consent and that we would not look at their troops as the enemy. So that's the mandate. Why would they ask for my consent if it were the way you put it now? If the parties do not give their consent, there can be no presence of foreign troops; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. And the original deployment, I think, to Sarajevo took place before -- there was an original presence there before March 1992. So that was when we had a status-of-forces agreement with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Belgrade, and that was the original basis for the headquarters. After that, we considered the government in Sarajevo to be the host nation and we entered into negotiations with them on a status-of-forces agreement. Of course as a practical matters, if your forces told us that they were going to shoot at us if we entered Serb territory, then we would not go unless we either had enough firepower or unless we had some -- some agreement. But the legal basis was first a mandate from the Security Council, and then in the second instance a status-of-forces agreement with Belgrade, and then, finally, a status-of-forces agreement with the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we were a part of this government in Sarajevo, one-third, that is with the right of veto. So you reached your agreement with us. We accepted your initial mandate; is that correct? Just yes or no. That is enough, so we can go home.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. All right. I'm afraid that you are not familiar about these legal matters, but let me tell you this: There is no chance for any UN formation to come to any territory without the agreement of the parties in conflict. That's how it was then. Later, Chapter 7 of the United Nations was amended, but I want to ask you something else. How did it happen that the UNPROFOR mandate be changed and that the powers of UNPROFOR be transferred to NATO without the decision of the Security Council? Are you familiar with the meeting in Naples between the UNPROFOR commander or the UN and the NATO forces commander for south Europe?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not transferred from UNPROFOR to NATO. I mean, I am reluctant to get into legal areas, but Resolution 836, paragraph 6, I think, but it could be 5 or 9, paragraph 6, I think, refers to regional organisations and gives them the authority to use force within the mandate given to UNPROFOR in specific circumstances. So, yes, it was an act of the Security Council which made a provision for NATO to be using force if needed in Bosnia and Herzegovina in support of the UNPROFOR mandate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're not going to agree about that. This was done at a meeting in Naples, and it bypassed the Security Council, but we will discuss this with someone else. Let us look at this document again here. It says in the penultimate paragraph that we were asking about small -- these journalists that we had arrested who were captured at Perucac Dam, Ognjen Tadic, and Mirko Pejanovic, and then it says: "The meeting was a valuable setting, the course for further contacts and negotiations. Karadzic seems particularly interested in finding acceptable solutions for Sarajevo stating that he would like to meet more often to discuss possible solutions." Do you dispute this document by Andreev or do you accept that that is Andreev's document dated from early 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, certainly what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly accept that this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we -- first of all, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at document 1D1074 in the e-court, please. And while we're waiting for the document, I am going to tell you what it is. It's a fax message from the European Community Monitor Mission. I'm sorry. I would like to leave this document for the private session. We will have two or three documents for the private session. Let's move to the next document then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was on my feet with regard to the private session, request for private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it this was not broadcast. Make sure. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I look at document 1D077 -- 1D1077.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also a fax message from the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia sent to Feissel from Ramcharan, and now this is actually a letter of the UN Secretary-General, which Ambassador Okun had seen and approved and gave his comments which were incorporated in the document. Can we look at page 2 of the document now. The date is the 27th of January, 1993. On page 2, the Secretary-General is informing Mr. Koch, Mayor Koch, as follows: "[In English] A shortage of arms is not the issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Unfortunately, notwithstanding the arms embargo, arms are still reaching all three sides. This may be seen in the fact that the armed forces of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina are now much better armed and have launched offensives in some areas that have put the Bosnian Serbs on the defensive." [Interpretation] Do you agree that it was the estimate of the Secretary-General that already in January 1993 there was no shortage of weapons and that the Muslim side, which is being referred to without justification as the government here because we also were part of the government, that they were well armed, that it was well around? This is before your time, yes, but this document we'll see, can we look at the next page. Anyway, did you know that this was the assessment of the Secretary-General already in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my doubts about this letter. First of all, it's not on UN letterhead. Seconds, it's not signed. Third, it's a -- it's -- the addressee is a private legal thing. I have not seen this document, and I have some doubts about it, but if what you're asking is about the contents, were we aware that weapons were flowing into Bosnia and Herzegovina to all sides, yes, we were aware of that. Yeah. I don't -- I doubt this is a genuine document. I would like to see the final signed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if it were to be shown that it is an authentic document, would you doubt the assessment of Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time I arrived, there was no doubt that weapons were flowing into all three sides, but overwhelmingly, by far, the best armed side was the Serbs and that would have been made clear in any communication, at least during the period where I served.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't asking about that. I was asking just about this letter. Can we look at this paragraph now. All three sides -- do you agree that the Secretary-General is receiving information from his associates out in the field, which included you later? How does the Secretary-General receive information? On the basis of your reports; isn't that right? Unless someone censors that in Zagreb or somewhere along the line to the Secretary-General. So he makes his assessment on the basis of the things that do reach him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite reluctant to comment until we establish whether this is a genuine document from Mr. Boutros-Ghali. I mean, I can try to answer if so directed by Their Honours, but it -- it doesn't feel right to me, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't like it. It's not that it doesn't feel right, Mr. Harland. Someone else will make the determination, but you don't like the document: "[In English] All three sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina have accepted the constitutional principles put forward by the co-chairmen in the Geneva Conference. The Bosnian Croat side has also accepted the map. The Bosnian Croat and the Bosnian Serb sides have indicated their willingness to cease hostilities while negotiations take place to iron out the provincial boundaries. The Bosnian government side has so far not indicated a willingness to end the hostilities." [Interpretation] Is it clear that already on the 27th of January, 1993, on St. Sava's day, accepted the constitutional principles and accepted that a cease-fire be introduced until negotiations are over and that the Muslim side did not do that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: These talks culminated in the so-called Vance-Owen Peace Plan. That peace plan was ultimately accepted by the Bosnian Croat party, by the Muslim party --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] May I -- may I --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're using up my time.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Bosnian Croat party, by the Bosnian Muslim party and was rejected by the Bosnian Serb party. What Boutros-Ghali, my boss, said about it while it was in negotiation, I cannot say. And I would like to see a signed version of his correspondence before entering into anymore detailed discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that all of that is superfluous. We are talking about the overall plan in May. What we're talking about here and what time interested in is: Is it clear to the Secretary-General already by the end of January that we accept the constitutional principles and cessation of hostilities? Did we accept that, does the Secretary-General know that, and is he distributing that information further? This is what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can comment about is what I saw. By the time I was there, your party had rejected the agreement. The other two parties had accepted the peace plan. I cannot comment on a letter unsigned, which looks wrong to me, which happened before my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the first page of this document. Mr. Harland, if you could help us who these persons are Ramcharan and Feissel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Bertie Ramcharan was, indeed, the assistant to Lord Owen, and I think that is an authentic signature. I know Mr. Ramcharan. But who the addressee is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document. It has an ERN number. I didn't make it up. I received it. I don't see that each telegram would have to have the general -- Secretary-General's signature. I am -- I'm tendering this document, and then I'm also asking for number 1076.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 174, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a similar document in front of us again. The operatives are the same. The document was also checked by Ambassador Okun and Mr. Ahtisarri and their suggestions were incorporated. The general -- the Secretary-General - can we look at page 2 now, please - is being given possible suggestions by Mr. Okun and Mr. Ahtisaari, because their positions are incorporated, possible talking points on meetings with high-ranking Turkish officials, and Turkey is a leading member of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, and so on and so forth. That's how it begins. And then we can go to page 4 of the document, please. This is an interesting document in which you can see that Turkey would get involved because President Ozal had stated that Bosnia would be part of the Turkish empire from the Balkans to the Chinese wall. Anyway, the suggestion is being made that he should tell the Turkish representatives -- all right we're going to read everything: "[In English] The Secretary-General could impress upon Turkish representatives that everything possible should be done to ensure that the Bosnian Presidency co-operates fully and faithfully with the co-chairmen in the Geneva peace process. Efforts to provoke foreign intervention are not helpful in this regard. The Secretary-General could also ask Turkish representatives to urge the Bosnian Presidency to accept the provincial map proposed by the co-chairmen as an honourable compromise. The provinces allocated to Bosnian Muslims gives them a substantial share of the industrial, mining, and energy resources of the country, something that has been bitterly criticised by the Bosnian Serbs." [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, do you dispute that the Secretary-General received briefings like this and talking points in preparations for meetings with Turkish officials, and that it is stated here that the Muslim side should be persuaded to accept the terms because they have a better deal than the Bosnian Serbs? We can finish this. Yes or no about these matters?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document. I don't know what he says, but these views expressed here are very consistent with those of Dr. Ramcharan, who was very wise and well informed, but we didn't always agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document. Perhaps I would have gotten on better with Mr. Ramcharan than you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D174.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document 1047, 1047.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, I'm not sure if we have the translation, but there is an ERN number there. This is a -- a trend or an occurrence that you probably would be familiar with. Sidorjenko, he's the commander of the Ukraine Nitnjan [phoen] Battalion. Lieutenant Bezrucenko, and so on, invited Siber for a meeting. And this is a document by the Muslim side. Sidorjenko says: "Are you aware of the incident of the 31st of July?" This is a document from 1992: "There is word that at an incident at the radar, one man was killed and four people were wounded." And Siber says: "I'm really sorry but I didn't know that anyone was killed until now." And Sidorjenko says: "I'm going to remind you of the circumstances. Your people moved the weapons in front of the radar, some 20 to 30 metres forward. In response, the Serbian side shelled that position and the consequence are -- are killed and wounded men. I don't know on what basis you attached yourself to the radar," and so on and so forth. Are you aware that Muslims, from the beginning to the end of the war, the Muslim army, used this trick to open fire at us from sensitive spots so that we would retaliate and then have our name blackened because of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of a Mr. Phillip Corwin? Is that name familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my boss after the departure of Mr. Viktor Andreev.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can keep this document. I would just like to read a document that I'm going to tender later. This is a letter from you to Philip Corwin and you write to him on the 30th of June, 1995, and you say: "[In English] Memo to Akashi --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have did in the e-court? Yes, this is a Prosecution document. Can we get that and we'll get this Siber document back. So it's Prosecution number 09848.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the cover page. You're writing to Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 of this document now, please. [Microphone not activated] "[In English] Update on the situation in Sarajevo and elsewhere. I referred to your memo to Mr. Akashi of this morning which seemed strange." [Interpretation] Well I'm surprised you advanced if you wrote to your superiors in this way: "[In English] In particular, you note that the Bosnian Serbs shelled the PTT building last night. Your conclusion was that UNPROFOR should protest to the Bosnian government." [Interpretation] And the following paragraph: "[In English] For your information, it is the opinion of acting commander Colonel Meille that the Bosnian army is not placing its mortars around the PTT building in such a way as to draw fire onto the building. Before commenting on aspects of the military situation in Sarajevo -- Sector Sarajevo, you might want to discuss the matter with Sector Sarajevo. You might also want to discuss the matter with me ..." [Interpretation] And then the last paragraph: "[In English] I would also appreciate if you could make it a practice to send me copies of the memoranda you write concerning the situation in Sarajevo. You will recall that I discovered about this memo and the last one you wrote the [sic] colleagues in Zagreb." [Interpretation] You are defending the Muslim side not only here, but you were defending it also before your boss who was working on the basis of information and documents. Why were you see interested to make the -- or to have the Muslim side look better than it actually was, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, yesterday when I was criticising the Muslims in one of these documents, you said that I was much fairer then. I had no agenda. I was simply commenting. This building that they're talking about, the PTT building, I worked -- that's my office. I was sitting in that building. Mr. Corwin, my boss, was not. He was sitting several kilometres away. Those shells landed on top of my office. It is true that there were Bosnian gun positions rather close. The city of Sarajevo is highly compact. It's interesting that when your gunners, who were very professional, I never deny that the Serbs were better soldiers. When they fired in, they didn't hit the Bosnian guns, they hit us. And when, in the previous document, you showed that there was a Bosnian gun position on the high ground near the Ukrainian mortar detecting radar, you hit the radar and you stopped us being able to defect who was firing future mortars, but you didn't hit the Bosnian gun. I was merely pointing this out to my boss, but I've become much more polite to my bosses since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, how precise does indirect fire need to be? Twenty or 30 metres off, is that something that would be acceptable for indirect fire? We don't have tomahawks for precise firing. For example, if the Muslim army approached the radar, do you think that we have such precise weapons to be able to differentiate our targeting for some 20 to 30 metres to adjust the aim practically.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is those shells landed directly on our office building. Colonel Meille, who you referred to, is the acting sector command. They dropped on the parking apron outside his office and blew out all his windows. So somehow your people managed to land a whole bunch of shells on our building without touching the Bosnian guns next door. The same way you managed to destroy the Ukrainian radar, which was trying to detect mortar shells, without mysteriously managing to hit the Bosnian gun next door. And there was this criticism of General Siber, who you unkindly referred to as a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, let me remind you. You do make an estimate about our officers' professionalism and qualification. You can not cite one single general whom we took out of prison and came him that rank, and there are some examples of that on the other side. But this is a people's army, just a regular man living in that area. You agree that this is a people's army. It's not a professional army. Some officers are professionals perhaps. The soldiers are not professionals. We are talking about old guns. And you will recall that your people concluded that the barrels were weakened by frequent usage, so a range or fluctuation in precision of some 20 to 30 metres is acceptable. I mean, it cannot be treated like a tomahawk. This is not a smart bomb that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad that you've at least conceded the point of the frequent usage of the Serb artillery guns. I thought you were going to deny even that. But they seemed to be able to hit the targets rather accurately when they wanted to. Our assessment, the assessment of our military colleagues, here we have Colonel Meille, the sector commander, the acting sector commander, making a -- an assessment that we were directly a target, but no doubt military experts are going to come in and talk about these things. Uh-oh; another bag of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it is you and Meille against Corwin. Corwin was your boss and I think that his assessment should not be neglected all together. However, we'll get to that as well, who fired, how often. Actually, since this has already been admitted, can we go back to 1047 now. Actually, 1048.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the number of 9848? We admitted them all, but the assigned number will be communicated to the parties in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record, it will be Exhibit P837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'd like to see the previous document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Let's just have it identified and then let's deal with 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the middle of the page now. No, no, no, 47. Let's have 47 first. 10 is 47. Mr. Sidorjenko says: "I have the protest of the Serb side to the effect that your weapons are being stationed in the Marsal Tito Barracks. Our information says that your weapons are 150 metres away from the Marsal Tito Barracks. Trust a colonel of the Ukrainian army. There was fire opened there at 9.00 this morning. It is possible that there are automatic guns mounted on vehicles and that they're on the move. They are your sniper shooters there on the roof who fire from time to time. I don't know who they're firing at and why. We ask that the sniper shooters be removed from the barracks." Mr. Harland, what -- what can be fired at from the top of the Marsal Tito Barracks except for the area that was called death alley; isn't that right, it couldn't have been anywhere else but the main street in front of the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume a military expert is going to answer that question, but my understanding is no, the snipers could fire, you know, at ranges up to a thousand metres which would give them from Marsal Tito Barracks some coverage into Serb areas like Grbavica which you were mentioning yesterday. But presumably military experts will come in to speak but I think that snipers can fire up to a thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But at Grbavica they could only see the tops of buildings. They couldn't see anyone down; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was asked about this earlier, I said that the main activity of snipers was shooting at each other, to try and stop each other from engaging, you know, the local population or soldiers. So the main sniper activity I ever witnessed was snipers moving from one high elevation to another, around the built-up area of the city, trying to remove each other from their nests. So I can imagine why Colonel Sidorjenko wouldn't have wanted them from -- firing from the top of the building he was based in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. This was the Marsal Tito Barracks, and the radar was another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. And there is a translation available which we can make available to the parties if it assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be helpful. Until that time, this will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is MFI D175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now have 1048, just in order to see that General Siber turned this into an order on the same day, on the 4th of August. He turned it into an order, and his order was to have artillery pieces moved 500 metres away at a minimum, and that includes those that are being overhauled. This is what he says: "I order the units of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at Sokol should be moved a minimum of 150 metres from the position of the UNPROFOR radar. "2. As for the barracks's Jusuf Djonlic and Marsal Tito, remove them at a minimum of 500 metres. This particularly refers to artillery pieces, including those that are being overhauled and Feroelektro. "3. Prohibit all use of fire from the mentioned barracks especially sniper shooters from the barracks of Marsal Tito," and then paragraph number 4, et cetera. So General Siber really did care about this because he issued an order to this effect on that very same day. Can it be admitted? Actually I just wanted to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that General Siber turned this into an order straight away as we can see here on our screens?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before and can't confirm it, and if the Bosnians really agreed to remove all of their weapons from a 500 metre radius of Marsal Tito Barracks, I mean, you could see on a map that if they did that around all UNPROFOR facilities or humanitarian facilities, there would be almost nowhere for them to put any weapons at all to defend themselves. So if they did it, it was a very generous act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection. And we have a translation available of that document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, can I show a document, 01038, which speaks in a concise fashion about the suffering of Serbs in Sarajevo from 1992 until 1994 on the basis of a statement made by a Witness 234/95/2. The ERN number is 06471071. Here it is. It has to do with Serbs primarily from Hrasnica and Hadzici. Actually, we better read it: "[In English] After spending two months in camps for Serbs first in the premises of the soccer club Famos, and then in the elementary school Aleksa Santic in Hrasnica, and then in the cultural centre in Hrasnica the witness was released. However, he had to report to the Green Berets military police. "This went on for three months during which time Muslim soldiers searched his flat nine times. Every time they confiscated his belongings and never gave him receipt. They searched his flat at night when they would beat and threaten him." [Interpretation] And further on it says that they were digging trenches: "[In English] Every day, each Serb member of that unit had a dig a trench two and a half metres long, 140 centimetres deep and 60 centimeters wide. Muslim and Croat soldiers made them carry their dead. [Interpretation] Muslim and Croat dead [In English] and the wounded from the first line, they were rarely allowed to go home and often were forced to stay for 15 days at the front line and dig trenches. "21 Serbs killed -- were killed and 13 wounded from the unit to which the witness belonged. The witness named most of them." [Interpretation] The perpetrators are members of the Green Berets in Hrasnica. Did you have any inkling of this or did you have any knowledge about the plight of the Serbs in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this document is, and I can't comment on it's authenticity. I have my doubts about how many Croat soldiers were in Hrasnica, but the general situation it's describing sounds believable, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would object to its admission on two grounds that it's irrelevant, Your Honour, and that we have absolutely no idea of the source or reliability of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, where is -- where is this from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from EDS, Your Excellency. This is the number, 06471071. I got this from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness was not able to speak about this document in any aspect, and the -- the provenance of this document is not clear at this moment. I have to confer with my colleagues, but speaking for myself, it's difficult to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's the Yugoslav committee for co-operation with the United Nations. It says U or, rather, YUSC. It was batch 151 that I received from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a summary of the witness, and the crux of the content of the statement was put to the -- to the witness and answered, and it was recorded into transcript. There's no further need to admit it separately. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 1039 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, Mr. Harland, may I inform you that that is a document from May 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the English version, please. I have the Serbian one, but this is an English version. Actually, sorry. English is 1036. Unfortunately, we have these different numbers there, but it can be admitted under one number, that is 1036. This is a weekly report from the Sarajevo area. 36, please. 1036. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now you see that. Let us have a look at what this weekly summary looks like. Look at the 15th of May. Explosions in the Grbavica area. Sporadic fire in Stup and so on. Then on the 16th of May, one Muslim soldier wounded near Rajlovac, and seven explosions in Grbavica. Sporadic fire near Smiljevici, Kromolj, Kobilja Glava. Now, on the 14th of May, explosions in Stup and Sedenik [phoen]. Sedenik is Muslim, Stup is Croatian. So, Mr. Harland, do we see here that there are mines exploding in Grbavica two or three days in a row, and also on the 17th of May there's an explosion at Grbavica. Grbavica is a Serb neighbourhood. It is Serb-held territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what you meant when you said that Serbs lived as if they were in Beverly Hills. Children ran across the street when they went to school not knowing whether they would be hit or not. There were blankets in the streets in order to stop snipers shooting, or at least obstruct it. Did you see that in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that the people of Grbavica had thousands and thousands of kilometres behind they could go to just behind the ridge where they would be safe, but, yes, I saw the blankets you describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will see from other documents how shells fell into Lukavica as well. So down here we see that -- look at the 18th of May. [In English] 20 mortar -- millimetre mortar on B and H side firing from Igman area. [Interpretation] So Muslims were at Igman and they were firing at Butmir. They were probably targeting a Serb area, but they held -- they hit one of their own territories; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 17th of May it says that UNMOs have SA fire and rifle grenades directed towards them. Protests made to 1st Corps of BiH. It was quite clear that that was the Muslim army that was firing; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: And which point, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second bullet point. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that appears to be an example of Bosnian government fire, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, perhaps under this number, 1036, the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a weekly summary of what, what organ, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: UNPROFOR. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D177.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1053, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Harland, it actually has to do with Annex 6, 6/674. The year is 1994. It's only two pages that I chose. You see that in front of you now, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 3056. "[In English] The city was without water. UNPROFOR said that it would take days to repair transmission lines downed in the fighting. UNPROFOR also said that the main power supply line (30 megawatts) between Reljevo and Buca Potok damaged in shelling before Christmas could not be repaired before mid-January while several days would be needed to obtain authorisation to repair the 18 megawatts -- megawatt line between Vogosca and Velesici. The power supply to the city was hit further by a technical halt ordered late on Tuesday at the Kladanj plant 50 kilometres to the north-west." [Interpretation] Actually, can we agree or disagree very quickly. There is no water because there is no electricity for the most part. There was no electricity because the transmission lines were broken during the bombing, and Kakanj is in Muslim hands; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that Reljevo is in Serb hands and Buca Potok in Muslim hands, and that the line between them was disrupted during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that Vogosca is in Serb hands and Velesici in Muslim hands?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the Secretary-General finds no fault of the Serbs here whatsoever. This is a pattern according to which Sarajevo runs out of water. We don't know why there was no power coming from Kakanj, but it can be seen that during the bombing around Christmas it was the lines between Serb and Muslim neighbourhoods that broke down and they would be repaired as they always were. Can I draw your attention to the next paragraph now: "[In English] Between B and H President Izetbegovic and Croatian President Tudjman." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the international community encouraged agreements between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR encouraged agreements between all of the warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the international community in general here, that they encouraged bilateral agreements between Croats and Muslims and that is how the Washington Accords came into being and also the federation was established later on that basis, too, but the Washington Accords happened right after -- or during their war, rather?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Americans were by themselves promoting the agreement between the Bosniaks and the Croats that became the Washington Agreement. When that agreement was signed, we participated and actively supported its implementation the way we would support any cease-fire agreement on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But look at this. Whenever Boban and I met in order to quell the fighting between Serbs and Croats, this sounded an alarm throughout the international community. Ah, it's the Serbs and Croats setting up a Christian Coalition at the expense of the Muslims. It was not a Christian Coalition. We saved many Serb and Croat lives in this way, and we invited the Muslims to join in such agreements. However, the international community would condemn that; isn't that right? Just yes or no. Do you remember that, that they were always watching us carefully so that we wouldn't do anything with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't remember. Now, further down, "Military activity," let's have a look at that: "[In English] ... UNPROFOR monitors counted 732 shells landing the city during the morning. Most of them in the Jewish cemetery area of the Grbavica district. Reporters who witnessed the combat from the Holiday Inn Hotel said that it was the heaviest fighting in weeks so close to the city centre." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the Jewish cemetery was guarded at Grbavica and that it was the Serbs that held Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this is exactly an example of the problem you raised about guns near the Marsal Tito Barracks. These front line positions that were being actively fought over were only a few hundred metres, both from urban residences in Grbavica and urban residences and UNPROFOR positions in the centre of Sarajevo. In Jewish cemetery is right in the urban -- the urban area. Very near in Holiday Inn Hotel, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do remember that the Serbs were not trying to extend their zone to Skenderija, whereas the Muslims kept hitting the Jewish cemetery in order to take Grbavica. So it's the Muslims who were shelling the Jewish cemetery in order to get to Grbavica; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jewish cemetery was very strongly fought over in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we agree on that, but what I'm trying to say is that the Serb side defended the entrance into Grbavica. They were not trying to attack. So what kind of offensive activity was taking place vis-a-vis Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a great deal of effort. You confirmed when we met at the prison Monday that there had been an initial fighting over Pofalici. You confirmed when we met that the Serb military had plans to advance as far as the Vojna Bolnice and some of those areas that were not realised. So all I would say is that this document confirms that there was very vigorous fighting right in the downtown area, and it gives us something of an answer to the questions that you were asking about where the Bosnian government side placed its heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, I'd like us to be very specific. I truly appreciate the baroque way in which you speak, but as far as criminal matters are concern, we have to be very specific. The Serb army did not want to go to Vojna Bolnice, the military hospital, it was the JNA, but the military hospital was a JNA hospital. So it's not the Serb army. It was the Yugoslav army at the very beginning when I was not in command at all, and actually I didn't even have an army of my own at the time. However, the fact remains that the Jewish cemetery was being attacked by the Muslims because we had no ambition of getting to Skenderija whereas they did have the ambition of getting into Grbavica. But let us leave that aside now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, can you answer the last question? I saw you nodding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, his last one was about whether the Serbs had the intention of getting into Skenderija versus whether the Bosnian had the intention of getting into Grbavica. I would say that our assessment was that both sides were actively militarily engaged in trying to improve their military positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a very quiet time of the war, I must say. I think we're talking about 1994, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that comment, the document will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the break be shorter? Is 15 minutes all right? Would that do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised impossible. I tried that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For planning purpose, Ms. Edgerton, how much would you need for your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My best estimate, Your Honours, is that I would need 45 minutes, and I'm confident I can conclude in under an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, it's not really worth disputing your credibility from the point of view of facts, but from the point of view of your assessments and feelings and sense of things, I would tend to dispute everything, so in the next hour and a half, I would like to do as much as possible on -- regarding this aspect. So the first question is: Are you here with the conviction that Markale was a Serb act? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two incidents at Markale, and on the first Markale massacre there were no conclusive empirical proof either way but some circumstantial evidence that pointed to the Serbs. The second Markale, there was an investigates which empirically demonstrated to the UNPROFOR commander that the shell was fired by the Serb, but this was disputed by one of our big artillery experts, Colonel Demurenko, who -- so again, it was not undisputed, but it indicated that it was probably the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You probably know that one of my generals was sentenced to a life sentence, General Galic that was, for among other things, Markale. According to the old Roman principle in dubio pro reo, so if you cannot prove, then you can convict based on suspicion. In any case, you explained this quite clumsily, and in your statement you said I said something about some body parts, and so on, that it was rather peculiar, and so on. Isn't that right? So now I would like to show -- this is what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like us to look at this footage and comment on Markale I. We're not ready for Markale II today, but we will do that at another time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play this tape. I have it now. Thank you. As it says here, we can see the Markale Market on a normal busy day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you can see what the normal busy day looks like. We can see people there and goods for sale, right? And now we can look at -- actually, do you agree that this is what a normal day at Markale looks like?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us look at Markale, how it looked on the 5th of February. This is around noon or sometime afterwards. It's a winter, early afternoon in Sarajevo. Let us see how Markale looked on that critical day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is before the explosion. That is leg, and actually those are the stalls, stands, where there is nothing on them, and this is an artificial leg before the explosion that would need to be planted somewhere, and this is a person getting angry because this limb has been left there. There are no people. There are no products. There is no explanation for the piling up of 400 people, 200 or over 200 whom were affected by the explosion. They have nothing to do at such a market. And now after the alleged explosion there is the leg that was blown off. Actually, this is the leg that we saw a little bit earlier. And look, there are no products, no produce on the stands. People are lying around. Here, this is a dummy, Mr. Harland. You will see. You don't have to comment on it now. You will see here they are loading up this dummy. This is a dummy. You will see that this is from the -- it's a mannequin used for shop windows. We asked for the name of that person. You can see how the leg just bends easily. You can see that. And now this is already the morgue. These are bodies from the front. We assert that these are bodies from the front. Look, let's go back. Let's go back a little bit. Here. Immediately after the explosion this person felt the most important thing was to pull out this plastic sheeting under this person that had been brought there. You can see how the body was on the plastic sheet. Now he is removing this sheet, and he's preparing the scene where our -- where the investigators are supposed to come, and you can see them dragging this body which was held somewhere for a very long time. The arm is stiff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop here. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise think point on the basis of a large number of assertions from Dr. Karadzic with respect to the events as he renders them in -- in this film, and I'd like to know the provenance of this film and the basis for these assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll let it go for a moment since I believe Mr. Harland is capable of dealing with this. But, Mr. Karadzic, can you answer the questions posed by Ms. Edgerton as to the provenance of this film?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This footage was filmed by the Muslim side, and evidently it was sold to somebody, or it was broadcast in an unedited version, and we recorded that from their television broadcast. And here you can clearly see the preparations. At later stages they broadcast only the edited footage where you don't see these preparations behind the scenes which are clearly showing that this is a very simple and inept fabrication. And this product is then brought to the courtroom, and Mr. Harland can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, you can probably say that this place with empty market stalls is where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before you proceed to put your question, how do we know this is broadcast -- this is broadcast by a Bosnian television station? Are you going to call a witness during the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think Mr. Harland saw that. Perhaps he didn't see this unedited footage, but he did see the edited footage when they're loading up the mannequin and pulling, drag that corpse. We are actually showing the unedited footage where you can see the -- the preparations for this whole fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, did you see that edited part of the footage?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I have on my screen is the logo of Serb Radio Television Sarajevo on the top right. This thing that says -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbian radio television was recording what the Muslim radio television was broadcasting. We didn't have any other way. They were broadcasting, and we were receiving that at Pale and were able to record it. Well, we have -- you have something else on the screen; is that right? Can we look at this again? What I am asserting here, Mr. Harland, is that this is a very old corpse of a soldier where the arm is still rigid. It's a totally dehydrated corpse, and it shouldn't have been dragged around like this without any respect. A freshly killed person, the corpse of such a person would not be dragged around like this without any respect and loaded onto a truck. And that dummy, we had asked from the Prosecution the name, the first and the last name and the autopsy results for that dummy being loaded up onto the truck from the Prosecution, and nobody can provide anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does Mr. Harland look at Markale in a slightly different way now that we have shown this footage?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this is exceptionally weird. I mean, you areal medical doctor, so I defer to you on that, but we sent a medical doctor as well, and as you can see even on this video, the place was very quickly filmed with UNPROFOR soldiers. We sent our commanding general, General Rose. You've given evidence from his book that he was by no means blindly sympathetic to the Muslims, and this -- this that you are suggesting is -- was never suggested by any credible or even incredible independent observer. I personally debriefed our medical doctor, Dr. Mucibaba. Nothing of what you are suggesting comes out. It shows to me a great distance from reality, and if this is taken from Srpska radio television Sarajevo, the CPT-SA in our script, then I would definitely want to look at the original unedited one because that is -- I mean, all the local television channels were extraordinarily manipulative and I would want to see the unedited footage. So I see this event completely differently, I have to say, on the basis our people present, General Rose, Dr. Mucibaba, and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the unedited version, which is one hour long. So I'm asking you, is this Markale, what you have seen now? Is this Markale? Do you see that the market stalls are completely empty?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That looked like Markale. When it is, what -- anything else about it I -- I can't say. All I can say is that I spoke to our medical doctor and our military commander, and none of them came up with any of this weirdness that you are now offering us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what Lord Owen said about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have the sound?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you dispute this too?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three investigations. The first and most immediate investigation indicated that they could not say for sure what distance it came from, but it came from the north-east, if I remember correctly, and that meant that it could have come from a Bosnian Muslim position or a Bosnian Serb position. We then had -- there were two more investigations. The only one I remember now is with a French force engineer who came from Zagreb, if I remember correctly. I read the report. I discussed it with him, and the balance of the evidence was, although still not a hundred per cent conclusive, was it probably came from Serb positions. I think at Poljine. I think Lord Owen -- I don't know what he was referring to. The document you showed was not a UN document, it was an EU document, but if Lord Owen was commenting, then he was almost certainly commenting on the first report from the same day, the UNMO report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 1046, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have a transcription of what Lord Owen said? I'm asking because it was not recorded into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter was translating. We couldn't get that report. Lord Owen is speaking on the basis of a secret report that was secret until the 12th of February, after which it was removed. On the 16th of February, the Secretary-General gave his letter to the Security Council, and now we are going to see that letter on the screen, and then for the 17th we're going to look at a letter, Prosecution document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the name -- the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- prepared by Mr. Harland about the same thing. There is no other footage of Markale other than the one that we saw. This was shown to the Muslim -- on the Muslim television. There is no other footage, and you know there must be some footage. Second, what Lord Owen said was up to the 12th and the report was secret, we are going to transcribe. Perhaps we will do it if nobody else can transcribe it. We're going to see, Excellency, the letter to the Security Council by the Secretary-General of the 16th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1046 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Harland, that we would agree that the Secretary-General is the highest authority within the United Nations; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the United Nations secretary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please. Yes. And now we can see the distance. The paragraph says: "[In English] The team has now submitted its report to my special representative with regard to the question of the origin of the 120-millimetre mortar shell. The report's findings are as follows: "The distance of origin of fire clearly overlaps each side of the confrontation line by 2.000 metres. Both parties are known to have 120-millimetre mortar -- mortars and bombs to go along with them. The team has no reason to believe that either party does not have access to the type of ammunition reported to the paragraph 12 of the report. There is insufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb in question could, therefore, have been fired by either side." [Interpretation] This is dated the 16th of February, 1994. After, as the Secretary-General says: "[In English] Initial investigation of the incident team established by special representative for former Yugoslavia to conduct a comprehensive follow-up investigation." [Interpretation] So the initial one that was hidden. And then the next one, comprehensive follow-up investigations, and then on the basis of that follow-up investigation, the Secretary-General asserted that it could not be established who fired it. Could we have the report by the Secretary-General tendere into evidence, please. Do you agree that this is a report by the Secretary-General? I mean it's quite well known.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it confirms what I said that the empirical evidence was inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D179, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 09632.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a Prosecution document dated the 17th of February. This is a draft by yourself and Andreev. Before that, do you recall that we asked to be part of the investigation both in the case of Markale I and Markale II, and that the Muslims did not allow that and we said that we would not accept any findings of the investigation in which our experts did not take part. Do you recall that, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall, because I personally asked, is both sides to allow us unhindered access to all places we needed to investigate and the Bosnia government side did give us unhindered access. And you have shown television footage which shows UNPROFOR soldiers on the site of the massacre and we then did our investigation, and your forces denied our people access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could we have denied you access to Markale when we don't control that? It's Muslim territory. How could we have denied access there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We wanted to have access to possible firing positions on both sides and to other sites, and we had unrestricted access to possible firing positions. We wanted to see where mortar plates could be placed, where these types of weapons were available, and the Bosnian government gave us that access and you did not, which made us a little suspicious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now you will see that that is incorrect. Can we please look at page 3 of this document, which was drafted by Mr. Harland and sent to Sergio De Mello by Mr. Andreev. Let's see. The middle one: "[In English] The circumstances surrounding the massacre at the Sarajevo marketplace on 5th of February, 1994, remain unclear. UNPROFOR has conducted a second and more thorough investigation into the incident. The result of the investigation, however, remains that it is not possible to determine from which side of the confrontation line the bomb was fired." [Interpretation] And now do you remember this? You wrote this. And now this is -- this corresponds to what you are saying now. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can we play the video footage where you can see that your expert had access to everything and that he toured everything and registered everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "First of all, I want introduce myself. I'm Captain Renka [phoen], Chief of Staff, Sector South Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. "I want to explain any details of the investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop the video for a moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is another year. If I'm not mistaken, this is the summer of 1995, not the winter of 1993/1994, but good try, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to rise on exactly that point. This film dates from the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see the weather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
